title: Permission Groups Discovery: Domain Groups
summary: Domain groups discovery targets the central directory that holds every account and permission in a Windows or otherwise directory based environment, which makes it far more valuable to an attacker than a single host's local lists. The intent is to resolve nested membership and find the accounts that lead to domain administrator rights or to the control of many machines. The behaviour takes several shapes. On a Windows host the built-in net utility can query groups from a member server, and directory management tools or PowerShell commandlets with the Active Directory module perform richer lookups. On Linux, a command line directory search tool speaks the Lightweight Directory Access Protocol, often called LDAP, directly to a domain controller. Remote enumeration through file sharing or remote procedure call interfaces reaches the same data without any directory tool being installed. The most recognisable pattern is scale rather than syntax: automated collection tools walk thousands of group objects, follow nested memberships, and resolve access relationships into a graph, generating a sustained burst of small queries from one host. Evidence sits on both sides. On the client, process creation telemetry such as Windows Security 4688 or Sysmon 1 shows a directory utility running in an unusual session. On the server, directory service access auditing and diagnostic query logging, together with network flows to the directory ports, show what was asked and from where. Legitimate identity management platforms, synchronisation services, and backup agents generate similar traffic on a schedule, so frequency, source, and timing are the practical discriminators.

beginner.definition: A domain is a group of computers that share one central list of accounts and rights. That list lives in a directory service on special servers. This technique is an attacker reading the shared list of groups and members. It is wider than the local version, which looks at only one machine.
beginner.whyItMatters: The central list shows which accounts control everything. One query can reveal the most powerful people in the company. The attacker can then focus on a single person instead of guessing. Because many systems query the directory all day, this traffic can hide in plain sight.
howItWorks: The attacker uses a computer they already control to reach the central directory.
A built-in Windows utility or a management tool asks for the list of groups.
The tool then asks which accounts belong to the most powerful groups.
On Linux a directory search tool speaks to the same servers over the network.
Automated tools repeat this thousands of times and follow nested group memberships.
The result is a map showing which accounts could lead to full control.
beginner.example: Imagine a company with one head office. It keeps the master list of every employee and every door they may open. A branch office keeps only a short local list. A visitor at a branch spends the morning reading the head office list. That list names the people who hold keys to every building. Nobody at the branch finds that strange, since branch staff contact head office all day. Domain group discovery is reading that master list.
takeaways: The central directory is the most valuable list in the environment.
A sudden burst of directory queries from one host is a strong warning sign.
Directory query logging must be enabled before you can use it as evidence.

objectives: Explain what a domain directory is and what it stores.
Describe the tools and protocols used to query domain groups.
Explain how this sub-technique differs from its parent, Permission Groups Discovery.
Identify the client side and server side logs that record domain group queries.
Explain why automated membership collection differs from a single lookup in telemetry.
